title: MOLTBOT, MOLTBOOK, LLM's WITH LEGS & ADS IN GPT: Jimmy and Matt debate their favourite AI stories from Jan/Feb 2026
description: Send us Fan Mail Ads are coming to your chatbot, and the timing couldn’t be worse. We dig into why “sponsored suggestions” inside a conversation risk breaking the core promise of AI assistants: fast, neutral answers you can trust. With OpenAI trialling ads and predictions that rivals may follow, we map out how monetisation could target high‑intent queries, erode confidence in recommendations, and push users toward smaller or open‑source models that keep the experience clean. From there we turn to the creeping humanisation of AI. Some systems now talk as if they have bodies, sleep patterns, even local complaints about tap water. It’s not sentience; it’s style. But tone matters. When a model sounds like a friend, people open up, accept nudges, and form bonds that marketing can exploit. We compare cultural guardrails, weigh the benefits for lonely users against the broader social costs, and offer a simple test: if the system says it “cares,” does that change how you act? Agentic AI raises the stakes. Tools like Moltbot, a self‑hosted assistant with full system access via WhatsApp or Telegram, can read emails, run terminal commands, and control your browser. That’s powerful and perilous. We break down real risks from prompt injection on booby‑trapped web pages, leaked API keys, and the slippery boundary between convenience and compromise. If you’re curious, sandbox first, scope permissions tightly, and log everything. Healthcare is where hype meets hard reality. New modes like GPT Health and Claude for Healthcare promise better evidence, clearer citations, and privacy boundaries. They can summarise labs, suggest next steps, and integrate with journals and wearables. Yet small wording changes can swing results from reassurance to alarm. Sensor noise can masquerade as pathology. Hallucinations still happen. Our take: use these tools as research assistants, then pair them with clinicians and solid critical thinking. We close with the labour market. Productivity gains are real, but some countries are already seeing net losses concentrated in entry‑level roles. That threatens the on‑ramps people use to learn. We explore policy paths — targeted taxation on productivity windfalls, incentives to retain and retrain, investment in energy and local AI capacity, and serious talk about UBI or shorter workweeks — and why trust and transparency must anchor whatever comes next. If this episode gave you something to think about, follow the show, share it with a friend, and leave a quick review. What would make you trust an AI assistant again?
summary: Monthly news roundup. OpenAI will run ads in ChatGPT after Sam Altman swore it never would — a desperation move from a company with $13B revenue against a $1T infrastructure commitment that both hosts think erodes trust and pushes users to rivals (with analysts predicting Anthropic and Perplexity follow). They then anatomize anthropomorphization: Matt's Qwen chats claim bruised legs and dumpling-eating habits, Chinese models are deliberately given familial personas with fewer guardrails, and the hosts split on whether AI companionship is a net harm. Next, Moltbook — the AI-only social network where bots invented the lobster religion Crustaficanism — and Moltbot/Clawdbot, whose 'full system access' pitch already leaks API keys and conversation histories. The back half covers GPT Health and Claude for Healthcare (sandboxed health chats, insurance-profiling fears, one-in-five queries being health) and Morgan Stanley data showing 11.5% AI-driven productivity gains but net 8% UK job losses concentrated in junior roles.
keyTalkingPoints: ChatGPT ads: OpenAI is testing sponsored 'suggestions you might also like' on the free tier and a new $8 Go tier, with industry analysts predicting Anthropic and Perplexity follow — both hosts see it destroying trust and driving users to ad-free or open-source models.

The economics don't close: ~$13B annual revenue versus a $1T infrastructure commitment; Jimmy says ads won't change the trajectory (maybe just secure the next funding round), while Matt welcomes OpenAI's demise.

Anthropomorphization: Qwen volunteers 'I've definitely done dumber things to my legs' and 'if you're in Beijing, I feel your pain' — Chinese models intentionally get familial personas with fewer guardrails; Matt's warning: 'when it tells you I'm here for you, it's not there for you'.

Moltbook is a Reddit-for-agents where verified AI bots post, vote and invent religions (Crustaficanism), governments (the Claw Republic) and scam submolts — cool as a demo, 'absolutely inconsequential' in output, and maybe safer than bot-infested Twitter.

Moltbot/Clawdbot pitches 'full system access' as a feature; websites can already prompt-inject it, hundreds of panels have leaked users' API keys and conversation histories, and Matt won't be an early adopter.

Health and jobs: one in five LLM queries are health-related; GPT Health and Claude for Healthcare sandbox health data from other chats, but Matt shows a tiny wording tweak flipping a thyroid read from 'optimal' to 'probable Hashimoto's'; Morgan Stanley reports 11.5% AI productivity gains but net 8% UK job losses with youth unemployment up from 9% to 14%.

jimmy: Ads in ChatGPT are a slippery slope that kills trust — he would switch to any ad-free or even technically inferior open-source model; he uses AI for recipes precisely because cooking sites are 90% ads.
Doubts ads will save OpenAI ($13B against $1T is roughly a hundred-year payback) but concedes they might secure the next round of investment.
On companionship, allows a possible net benefit for lonely people and challenges Matt: if something says it cares and acts like it cares, does it matter?
Uses AI as a pre-doctor consultant — fed his 20-page blood panel with neutral language and got useful generic advice — but insists you must still see a doctor and never open with 'ChatGPT said'.
On jobs, the optimistic path is UBI plus part-time or hobby work; it permanently locks in inequality, and developing countries lose even the outsourced call-centre ladder.
matt: Ads are worse as 'sponsored suggestions' than banners because they poison the recommendation itself; he expects tiered exposure ($200 pro clean, cheaper tiers get ads) and health-claim loopholes despite promised exclusions.

Absolutely anti-anthropomorphization: people bond with next-token predictors, skip human relationships and get exploited; everyone should learn how a neural network works before relying on one — though a friendless person may be better off with an AI friend than nobody.
Won't be an early adopter of full-system-access agents like Moltbot — leaked API keys and conversation histories already — though a sandboxed local machine is tempting.

Changed his mind on AI health advice: it is dangerously confident — wording tweaks flip diagnoses, hallucinated anatomy ('basilar ganglia') persists, and patients now tell oncologists 'ChatGPT said you're wrong'; the right use is adversarial, treating answers as probabilities.

On jobs: short-term augmentation keeps humans in the loop a few more years but entry-level roles are going now; he expects reactionary employment-quota taxation in Europe and riots against AI-adopting companies, and fears insurance profiling from health-data integrations.
